hikes.coachNote: The diagnostic result the entire plan was built around — summited at 10,817 ft with no altitude symptoms, where a prior attempt turned back at 13k. The 'vegetable' descent was a ~2,000 cal deficit plus ~5.5L fluid deficit, not a fitness ceiling. Fueling nearly broke you; the engine is there. The 90 F reading on the map matters: heat is the reason the sweat loss was so extreme, and Idyllwild in early August will not be cooler.

Two flags. Sweat loss 5,115 ml for only 1,342 ft of climbing is the dry-thin-air tax at altitude, and you were again splitting water three ways. And needing to stop at every rise at 10-11k is the third time altitude has cost you something.

hydrationAnalysis.sodiumFinding: On San Jacinto ~1,900 mg sodium replaced vs ~7,000-9,000 mg lost. Peeing 4x while dehydrated points at LOW SODIUM, not excess water — kidneys dump water they can't hold.
hydrationAnalysis.volumeFinding: Drinking large volumes at rest stops outpaces absorption. Sip small and frequent; alternate plain and electrolyte bottles.
hydrationAnalysis.correction: 2 electrolyte tabs in 1L is the same concentration as 1 in 500ml — concentration was never the issue, total sodium was.
hydrationAnalysis.flagToDoctor: A very salty sweat rate is worth raising with a doctor.

fuelingProtocol.strategy: Front-load solid food in hours 1-4 so gels are not doing rescue work at hour 8. Mix through the middle, gels freely on descent.
fuelingProtocol.keepGelsReason: Gels were what made the San Jacinto descent survivable. The fix is MORE total calories spread earlier, not fewer gels.
swapOut: Costco trail mix (fiber + dried fruit ferments)

bladderDrawbacks: No volume feedback — you cannot see how much you have drunk, which is one plausible reason intake has stayed low without you noticing.

Hose and bite valve freeze. This is a classic Whitney summit-morning failure: pre-dawn start at 12,000 ft in October, hose freezes, and you cannot drink at all for hours.
freezeMitigations: Blow air back down the hose after every sip so no water sits in the line.
Insulated hose sleeve, or run the hose inside a jacket layer.
Simplest option: use insulated bottles rather than the bladder on summit morning.
Sleep with the bladder and bottles inside the tent, not in the vestibule.
waterCarry.recommendation: Keep the 2.5L reservoir for plain water and add roughly 2L of bottle capacity for electrolyte mix. That reaches ~4.5L total, solves the alternating-fluid problem, gives you visible feedback on intake, and gives a freeze-proof fallback for summit morning.

diamoxTrial.status: prescribed, 20 days supply — trial not yet done
diamoxTrial.why: You are the one person in this log with a documented fluid and sodium deficit on every long effort, and acetazolamide is a diuretic. Meeting its effects on a low-stakes day rather than at hour eight of a sixteen-mile hike is worth the small delay.
diamoxTrial.whenToTrial: This week, at home or before a short local walk. Not on Devils Slide.
logThese: Tingling (paraesthesia) — where, how strong, how long it lasted. Fingers, toes and around the mouth are the usual spots.
Taste changes — especially with anything carbonated, which classically turns metallic.
Urination — how many extra trips, and crucially HOW MANY HOURS after the dose. You will be taking this while sleeping at 12,000 ft, and repeated 2am trips out of a tent cost sleep you cannot spare.
Drowsiness, nausea, or appetite change — all would compound your existing fuelling problem.
Whether your actual electrolyte drinks still taste acceptable ON the drug.
diamoxTrial.criticalTest: Taste your real on-trail drinks — Liquid IV, salt tabs, whatever you plan to carry — while on Diamox. If the drug makes them taste metallic you will drink less, which is the exact opposite of what you need. Far better to discover that this week and swap products than at Trail Camp.
questionsForDoctor: Start date: the plan says Sep 30, but you sleep at ~10,000 ft at Cottonwood on Sep 29. Should it start a day or two earlier so that night is covered?
Electrolytes: acetazolamide causes potassium loss, and you sweat 690-950 ml/hr with historically low sodium replacement. Any specific guidance or monitoring they want?
Sulfa: acetazolamide is a sulfonamide derivative — confirm no history of sulfa reaction.
Whether the two mild altitude episodes and the very salty sweat rate change anything in their plan.

beetProducts.ingredients: Beet, celery, cucumber, carrot, apple, spinach, ginger, lemon juice
beetProducts.note: Using it at home rather than carrying it is the right call — 450 g of perishable liquid up 3,700 ft was never worth it. Nitrate content is plausibly meaningful: the ⅓ lb of spinach may contribute as much nitrate as the beets, since spinach is among the highest-nitrate vegetables by weight.

beetProtocol.plan: One bottle Friday Jul 31, one Saturday Aug 1 before the Devils Slide hike.
beetProtocol.timing: Plasma nitrite peaks roughly 2–3 h after drinking, so Saturday's bottle wants to go down about 2–2½ h before the trailhead — which lines up with the breakfast slot already in the week plan.
beetProtocol.takeWithFood: Drink it WITH breakfast, not on an empty stomach in the car. The mocha-on-an-empty-stomach mistake on Jul 11 produced exactly the bloating you are trying to avoid, and this bottle carries 5 g of fiber plus apple and carrot fructose.
beetProtocol.fridayIsTheTest: Friday's bottle doubles as a tolerance test 18 hours before it matters. Note any reflux, gas or bloating and how long after drinking it appeared.
beetProtocol.decisionRule: If Friday produces reflux or significant gas, SKIP Saturday's bottle. Two inches of ginger per bottle is more than the Sol-Ti that already gave you reflux, and you have said ginger is always a no. Trading a marginal 3–5% oxygen-efficiency gain for reflux at hour two of a twelve-hour hike is a clearly bad deal.
beetProtocol.countsTowardCarbs: 36 g carbs and 150 cal per bottle — real numbers against Friday's and Saturday's targets, not free extras.
beetProtocol.diamoxSynergy: 1,010 mg of potassium per bottle (20% DV) is a genuine bonus if you are on Diamox, which causes potassium loss. This is the one way the two plans help each other.
beetProtocol.expectations: Do not expect to feel anything. You ran SuperBeets ~30 days and felt nothing, and two bottles is acute dosing rather than the 3–7 day loading that shows the clearest effect. Whatever this does, it is a rounding error next to hitting your fluid, sodium and calorie targets.
beetProtocol.harmlessSurprise: Beeturia — pink or red urine, sometimes reddish stool — is common after beet juice and completely harmless. Worth knowing in advance so you do not mistake it for blood mid-hike.
beetProtocol.fridayResult: PASSED. No reflux from the beet juice, from cold coffee, or from the 35 mg caffeine gel. Saturday's bottle is a go.
beetProtocol.coffeeCaveat: One distinction worth keeping straight: reflux and bloating are different problems. The Jul 11 trouble was bloating and gas from a MOCHA on an empty stomach at 5am — milk plus fasted gut plus heat. No reflux from cold coffee is genuinely good news, and cold brew is lower in acid than hot brewed, so it fits. But it does not clear coffee of the bloating question. If you want it Saturday, have it with breakfast rather than fasted, and skip the milk.
beetProtocol.nitrateTiming: Plasma nitrite peaks roughly 2-3 hours after ingestion, so on a hike day the beet dose belongs 2-3 h before the start rather than the night before or at the trailhead. For a 6 am start that means taking it around 3-4 am, which in practice means with the pre-drive coffee and food, not in the car park.
beetProtocol.doseUnknown: SuperBeets does not declare milligrams of nitrate on the label. The exercise literature uses roughly 5-8 mmol, and there is no way to tell from the tub how close one teaspoon gets. Beetroot juice is the more verifiable route if the nitrate effect is the reason for taking it at all.

gearNote: This list is what has come up in conversation, not a full kit audit — insulation layers, gloves, a warm hat, sleeping bag and pad for a 12,000 ft October night may already be sorted. Worth a full gear shakedown on the Aug 22 loaded hike.

openIssues.issue: Carrying food is not eating food — dates were carried unused on Aug 2
openIssues.action: He carried dates the whole way and ate none. That reframes the Aug 2 shortfall: it was not a packing failure, it was an execution failure, and no shopping list fixes it. Five gels over 11.6 h is one every 2.3 hours — the 45-minute recurring Time alert on the Fenix either was not set or was not obeyed, and that alert is the entire mechanism. Three concrete changes: set the alert and treat it as non-negotiable; put the next two items in a HIP-BELT pocket, not the pack, because anything requiring a stop and a shoulder-strap removal does not get eaten; and pre-open the dates into a single ziplock so eating one is a one-handed action while walking.

openIssues.issue: Ran out of gels near the summit — the pivot of the whole day
openIssues.action: His own words: as soon as the GU ran out he was thinking about how to get down. Five gels over 11.6 h is 105 g of the 289 g total, and the supply ended before the effort did. Carry more than feels necessary — the marginal weight of two extra gels is 80 g against 13.2 lb of water. This is the single cheapest fix available.

openIssues.issue: The 40 g bar is fat and fibre wearing a fuel label
openIssues.action: 200 cal for 9 g of net carbohydrate, two thirds of it fat, 6 g fibre, and a gastrointestinal-discomfort warning on the flap which normally means sugar alcohols. One slice of ordinary sandwich bread gives 18 g net for 110 cal. Drop the bar from the trail list; it is also a live suspect for the 9,700 ft stomach event. Third bread-or-bar in this project counted as carbohydrate while delivering almost none — 1 g, 9 g and 18 g net respectively.

openIssues.issue: Carrying 6 L of water costs 13.2 lb
openIssues.action: He carried 6 L and drank 5.5. Water alone was 13.2 lb — 45% of the 30 lb Whitney Day 1 target, spent on something the GRAYL can refill. Carry 4.5 L and plan a filter stop. The pack felt heavy because it was, and most of the weight was replaceable.

openIssues.issue: Wanting to stop training arrived with an empty tank
openIssues.action: At 9,000 ft, 1,723 kcal behind burn, he questioned whether to do Whitney at all. Then he walked the last three miles at 22, 21 and 23 minutes. Low carbohydrate availability degrades mood and judgement directly — the thought tracked the fuel, not the fitness. Worth recording so the next time it happens it is recognised as a symptom with a known cause, the same way the calf cramp was.

openIssues.issue: Jul 30 hit the carb target, but by a route that will not repeat
openIssues.action: First day on record to reach the carb target: ~398 g net against 365-511. Worth noting how. Roughly 138 g came from 500 g of weighed rice at lunch and 176 g net from a feast dinner carrying about 88 g of fat. Total fat for the day was around 118 g and calories around 3,550. That works once. It is not a Friday template: tomorrow's load target is 511-730 g, which is more carbohydrate than tonight delivered, and fat at that level crowds out the volume needed and slows everything down. The repeatable route is the LUNCH pattern — weighed rice with dhal — run twice, plus juice and dates. Fried food is the wrong tool for a load day.

openIssues.issue: Fried, late and high-fat two nights before a 16 mi day
openIssues.action: Deep-fried vadai, mutton curry and chilli chicken together put roughly 88 g of fat in one evening meal, against a standing record of reflux and of gut distress on long efforts. Nothing to do about it tonight. The thing to actually check is tomorrow's morning glance: sleep score and hours against the recent run. If sleep drops, that is the cost, and it lands on the load day before Saturday.

openIssues.issue: Ginger in the Trader Joe's juice — tested, no reaction
openIssues.action: Escalated after reading the front label. This is not a trace: the bottle states TWO INCHES of ginger per 450 ml serving, roughly 20-25 g of fresh root — more than most recipes use for a whole dish. His own record says he has acid reflux and that ginger is a trigger. It sat sixth in the ingredient list, which is why the back label made it look incidental. Stop using this one on Friday and Saturday. The Pressed orange+beet juice lists only orange and beet, so that is the hike-day drink. Whether to keep this as a weekday drink is his call, but it should be a decision rather than an accident.
openIssues.resolution: Overstated on my side and corrected by him. It is not a daily drink — it is taken only on hike days, and he had it once before with no problem. Today it has been an hour and a half to two hours with nothing. So the ginger dose in this form, juiced and diluted among 450 ml of other vegetables, does not trigger his reflux at this quantity. The label told me the dose; it could not tell me the response, and the response is his data, not mine to infer. Same rule as Garmin versus the PDF, pointing the other way: he owns how it felt.

openIssues.issue: Beet sources overlap on hike days; total nitrate still unknown
openIssues.action: Corrected: the Trader Joe's bottle is hike-day only, not daily, so the three-way overlap is narrower than it looked. What stands is that none of the sources declares nitrate, so the dose cannot be checked against research. The front label helps — 1¼ beets plus ⅓ lb of spinach, and spinach is among the highest-nitrate vegetables there is. The actionable part is timing rather than quantity: take it 2-3 h before the start, since plasma nitrite peaks around then.

openIssues.issue: The diet is low-carb by composition, not by accident of tracking
openIssues.action: Four labelled items on Jul 30: bread 1 g net carb per slice, sardines 0 g, tea 1.5 g, juice 25 g. Three of the four are near-zero carb, so the juice was the entire carbohydrate intake of the morning. This is not a measurement problem — it is what is being chosen. A low-carb pattern is a legitimate way to eat and is directly at odds with nine consecutive weekends of 16-25 mi days on a roughly 1,800 kcal glycogen tank. It is the most economical explanation for intake landing near half of burn on San Jacinto, and for the stopping on inclines. Fixing it means adding rice, dosa, poha, dates and juice deliberately, not tracking better.

openIssues.issue: The bread is a fibre supplement, not a carbohydrate source
openIssues.action: Inked Bread is 11 g total carb and 10 g fibre per 27 g slice, so 1 g net carb and 30 calories. Three slices read as 33 g of carbs and deliver 3 g. This is the likeliest single reason intake keeps landing near half of burn: the tracking was counting fibre as fuel. It is a good bread for protein (4 g) and sodium (140 mg) per slice, and a poor one for loading. Swap it for rice, dosa, poha or dates on Friday load days and on the trail. Also worth noting 3 slices is 30 g of fibre in one sitting, which is a full adult day's worth, and there is a standing gut-distress issue on long efforts.

openIssues.issue: Bilateral calf cramp two days before a 16 mi hike
openIssues.action: Both calves, at rest, the morning after an hour in a 20 lb vest — new load on the calves, on the back of a day with 2 L of fluid and no added sodium. Two Liquid IV sticks is a sensible response, roughly 1,000 mg of sodium. Watch whether it clears before Saturday. Cramp that becomes one-sided, or comes with swelling or pain in a single leg, is a doctor call and not a dashboard one.

openIssues.issue: Pulse oximetry is off — no SpO2 baseline before an altitude objective
openIssues.action: 3 readings in 304 days. Enable Pulse Ox on the Fenix now (Health & Wellness > Pulse Ox > All Day or During Sleep) so nine weeks of sea-level baseline exist before Cottonwood. Free, and it is the one sensor that speaks directly to how altitude is being tolerated.
openIssues.resolution: Pulse Ox enabled during sleep on the Fenix on Jul 28. A baseline will build on its own from here — no action left.

openIssues.issue: Sleep drops to about 3 hours after every long effort
openIssues.action: Across the six longest days the night-of average is 3.4 h against 6.8 the night before. Whitney has summit day depending on sleep at 12,000 ft immediately after a 3,700 ft climb. Finishing Day 1 early, fuelling properly and taking no caffeine after midday are the levers.

openIssues.issue: Diamox tolerance not yet tested
openIssues.action: Prescription and 20 days of supply confirmed, so a trial costs nothing from the trip stock. Do it this week at home or before a short local walk rather than on Saturday's big hike — acetazolamide is a diuretic and you already run 1.5-5.5L fluid deficits with far too little sodium. Log the timing of the urination effect and taste-test your actual electrolyte drinks while on it.

openIssues.issue: Diamox start date may not cover the Cottonwood night
openIssues.action: Plan says start Sep 30, but you sleep at ~10,000 ft on Sep 29. Ask the prescriber whether to start a day or two earlier.

openIssues.issue: Devils Slide permit faxed, awaiting confirmation
openIssues.action: Follow up with the San Jacinto Ranger District (909) 382-2921, open Thu-Mon. Marion Mountain is the fallback and was not quota-flagged the way Devils Slide is — but it still needs its own wilderness permit. Adventure Pass ($5/day) required for Humber Park parking.

openIssues.issue: Never carried more than a 12 lb pack — Whitney Day 1 needs roughly 30 lb
openIssues.action: Progressive loading: 18 lb on Aug 1, 22-25 lb on Aug 15, 28 lb late Aug, full weight in September. At 161 lb that is 7.5% rising to 18.6% of bodyweight — inside normal backpacking range, but it changes HR, pace and knee load on the 6,200 ft descent.

openIssues.issue: Sleeping height still steps up 3,400 ft on the night before the summit
openIssues.action: Highest slept is 8,600 ft, two nights in Mammoth Lakes. Trail Camp is 12,000 ft, a 3,400 ft step. Two things now close most of it: the Cottonwood Camp night on Sep 29, and the High Creek Camp permit in Week 7 of the plan on Sep 12, which sits around 9,000-9,600 ft. Taking the Week 7 overnight rather than making it a day hike is what turns this from an open risk into a rehearsed one.

openIssues.issue: No big day followed by another big day
openIssues.action: Back-to-back days are not the gap — the data has eight consecutive-day pairs, including Jul 25–26. What is untested is a long day followed by another long day: Jul 25–26 was 2.8 h then 5.7 h, where Whitney is roughly 6.6 h with a full pack then a 4 am start for 14,505 ft. Week 7 of the plan (Sep 12, permit at High Creek Camp) is the one scheduled chance to rehearse it, because camping mid-route forces a second day on tired legs.

openIssues.issue: Two clear mild episodes at 10,500-11,000 ft, plus one that resolved
openIssues.action: REVISED DOWN from three: San Jacinto clumsiness at 10,500 ft (Jul 18) and unacclimatised gondola dizziness at 11,053 ft (Jul 25) are altitude-relevant. Gem Lakes discomfort (Jul 26) was mild, acclimatised and resolved. The Jul 24 Whitney Portal headache moves out of this column entirely — it is eyestrain, not altitude. Still worth raising with your doctor alongside the Diamox plan.

openIssues.issue: Diamox is a diuretic and you already run a fluid and sodium deficit
openIssues.action: Raise this interaction explicitly with the prescribing doctor, and do the trial run in August — not on Sep 30 — so side effects are known before summit week.

openIssues.issue: Blurry vision — 1.25 readers likely under-corrected
openIssues.action: Optometrist visit being arranged, which is the right answer. Three things worth telling them: you are going to 14,505 ft in October, you will need to read a watch and map in the dark on summit morning, and whether the blur is only close-up or at distance too. Ask about proper high-UV sunglasses while you are there — UV at 14,000 ft is far stronger than at sea level and granite and snow reflect it back at you. Carry a SPARE pair of correct-strength readers — losing your only pair at Trail Camp with a map and a stove to manage is a real problem.

openIssues.issue: Poles left at home on both Mammoth hikes
openIssues.action: Low cost on flat family hikes, but the Jun 20 A/B proved poles are worth ~10 bpm. Make them automatic.

openIssues.issue: Own fluid intake unrecorded on both Mammoth hikes — you were the family's water carrier
openIssues.action: Carry and log your own bottle separately from the shared supply. Sweat loss was 2,677 ml and 5,115 ml on those two days.

openIssues.issue: Total sodium far too low on long efforts
openIssues.action: Raise to 700-1000 mg/hr; test on next hike

openIssues.issue: Calorie intake ~50% of burn on long days
openIssues.action: 250-300 cal/hr front-loaded

openIssues.issue: Coordination loss (clumsiness) at ~10,500 ft
openIssues.action: Likely fuel-driven, but ataxia is a descend-now sign. Brief your hiking partner to watch for it. Retest on a well-fueled second San Jacinto.

openIssues.issue: Gut distress after long hikes (bloating, gas)
openIssues.action: No coffee on hike mornings, swap trail mix for dates/rice. Mention to doctor given reflux history if it recurs every long hike.

openIssues.issue: Left shoulder blade pressure during exertion
openIssues.action: Single occurrence, likely uneven strap load. Mention to a doctor if it recurs or spreads.
openIssues.resolution: One week only, at a load he was not conditioned for and probably with the pack poorly set up. Did not recur.

openIssues.issue: VO2 max 37 vs October target 41-42
openIssues.action: Zone 2 volume + one weekly interval session. Prefer incline treadmill 10-15% or uphill hiking intervals over running, given back/hip flexor history.

openIssues.action: Switched to %HRR. Still calibrate altimeter at known elevation and enable multi-band GPS.
openIssues.resolution: Not needed. Satellite selection is on auto and ±50 ft of barometric drift is acceptable for this purpose. Zones were read directly from Garmin's own configuration rather than assumed.

openIssues.action: Reopens September. Baldy and a second San Jacinto carry August altitude work.

openIssues.action: Book on Recreation.gov

openIssues.action: Big Agnes Copper Spur UL1 is owned; the MSR Access 2 is the partner's suggestion for a shared tent, to be settled at the Labor Day sale on Sep 7. Week 7 on Sep 12 is the only scheduled night out before the summit, so a tent bought on Sep 7 gets exactly one rehearsal — pitching, condensation, and whether two people and two packs actually fit. If the decision slips past Sep 12, go to Whitney with the tent already known to work rather than the one bought on offer.

openIssues.issue: Reflux under a loaded pack and lying at Trail Camp is still untested
openIssues.action: The juice is now tested at rest and on a hike day with no reaction, which settles the ordinary case. The condition that has not occurred yet is the specific one: a hipbelt compressing the abdomen under roughly 30 lb, ten hours of exertion, and then lying down at 12,000 ft. Exertion and recumbency both raise reflux risk independently of what was drunk. Not a reason to change anything now — a reason to notice it on the Week 7 overnight, which is the rehearsal for exactly that combination.

forwardPlan.title: Buy the fuel and fix the filter before Aug 15
forwardPlan.detail: Order Precision Fuel drink mix and PF 30 gels — 4 plain, 2 caffeine. Buy a CNOC Vecto 3 L bag to run gravity through the Sawyer instead of pressing the GRAYL. Add LMNT sticks. Book Cottonwood Camp for Sep 29 if not already done.

forwardPlan.title: San Gorgonio via Vivian Creek
forwardPlan.detail: 19 mi, 5,400 ft, summit 11,503 ft. Permit secured. Highest point in Southern California and a new altitude record on foot. Biggest day of the plan so far.
forwardPlan.targets: Fuelling rehearsal 2 on the Precision Fuel plan: 41 g carb/hr and 825 mg sodium per litre, against 25 g/hr and 539 mg/L on Aug 2. Falsifiable test — does stopped time drop below 40%? It went 54.6% to 46.5% between Jul 18 and Aug 2.

forwardPlan.title: Recovery + strength
forwardPlan.detail: Hip flexor routine Monday. Two strength circuits. One Zone 2 ruck 45-60 min at 18 lb. One incline-treadmill interval session at 10-15% if the back and hips are quiet.

forwardPlan.detail: You said no hike, which is the right call between two big efforts. Rather than nothing: one 60-75 min Zone 2 ruck at 20 lb plus a strength circuit keeps the load line from dropping off a cliff.

forwardPlan.title: San Gorgonio via Vivian Creek
forwardPlan.detail: 19 mi, 5,400 ft, summit 11,503 ft — the highest point in Southern California and a new altitude record on foot. Permit secured. Biggest day of the plan so far and the closest analogue to Whitney Day 1 and Day 2 combined.
forwardPlan.targets: Fueling rehearsal #2, this time on a day long enough that failure shows. Expect 10-12 hours. Free permit required in advance from permits.sgwa.org.

forwardPlan.title: Load-focused local hike
forwardPlan.detail: Blue Sky to Potato Chip Rock, ~10 mi. The point is pack weight, not distance or speed — this is where you find out what 28 lb does to your descent.

forwardPlan.title: OPTIONAL: one more night near 10,000 ft
forwardPlan.detail: Car camp at Horseshoe Meadow (~10,000 ft) and day hike Cottonwood Lakes. Downgraded from high priority now that two nights at 8,600 ft are on the board — your sleep ladder is already 8,600 to 10,000 to 12,000 rather than a cold jump. Still the single best value weekend available if the calendar allows, because it also rehearses the Sep 29 Cottonwood night on a night that does not matter.
forwardPlan.targets: Second Diamox trial if the first went fine — this time at a sleeping altitude where the drug is actually indicated.

forwardPlan.title: El Cajon Mountain — reopened
forwardPlan.detail: 11.2 mi, 3,589 ft. Steep, hot, relentless. Carry full intended Whitney Day 1 weight.

forwardPlan.title: Week 7 — the keystone weekend
forwardPlan.detail: San Gorgonio via Vivian Creek, 25 mi and 7,500 ft, with the overnight permit at High Creek Camp and a double summit. This is the only session in the plan that tests all three untested things at once: a full pack, sleeping high at roughly 9,000–9,600 ft, and a big day on legs that already did a big day. Take the overnight rather than converting it to a day hike — the camp is the point.

forwardPlan.title: Last big effort
forwardPlan.detail: San Gorgonio again with full pack, or Baldy. Whatever happens here, the taper starts Monday regardless — resist the urge to cram in late fitness.

forwardPlan.title: Taper
forwardPlan.detail: Volume down roughly half, intensity light, sleep treated as training. One short flat 5-6 mi hike on the 26th or 27th. No new gear, no new foods.

forwardPlan.title: Travel and pre-load
forwardPlan.detail: Drive up. Hydrate deliberately, salt food generously, eat carbohydrate-heavy. No alcohol.

forwardPlan.title: Cottonwood Camp — sleep ~10,000 ft
forwardPlan.detail: Recreation.gov reservation required. Easy walking only. This is the acclimatization night the whole schedule is built around.

forwardPlan.title: Light acclimatization + Diamox start
forwardPlan.detail: Short hike, no summit ambitions. Start Diamox only as your doctor directs — and only if the August trial run went fine.

forwardPlan.title: Whitney Portal to Trail Camp
forwardPlan.detail: ~6 mi, 3,700 ft to 12,000 ft with full overnight pack. Target Zone 2, arrive with reserves. Filter water at Outpost or Trail Camp. Eat and drink on the clock even if appetite is gone — this is the exact day San Jacinto warned you about.

forwardPlan.title: SUMMIT DAY
forwardPlan.detail: Trail Camp to summit 14,505 ft via the 97 switchbacks and Trail Crest, then all the way down. Roughly 2,500 ft up and 6,200 ft down. Brief your hiking partner on the descend-now signs before you start: coordination loss that does not improve with rest, headache unrelieved by fluid and food, vomiting, breathlessness at rest, confusion.

measureThis.title: Weigh yourself before and after the hike
measureThis.why: Every sweat-loss number in this whole project is Garmin's model estimate, not a measurement. Pre- and post-hike bodyweight is the real thing: roughly 1 kg lost equals 1 litre of net fluid deficit. One bathroom scale, two readings, and we finally know whether 822 ml/hr is accurate or whether we have been planning around a number that is 30% off.
measureThis.how: Weigh first thing, minimal clothing, before eating or drinking. Weigh again immediately on getting home, before rehydrating further. Note both, plus total fluid drunk and total sodium taken.

respiratoryTrainer.device: Generic respiratory resistance exerciser (adjustable inspiratory/expiratory resistance, bite mouthpiece)
respiratoryTrainer.verdict: Worth doing. Low risk, cheap, plausible benefit — but small, and it must not displace the things that actually decide this trip.
respiratoryTrainer.whatItDoes: Inspiratory muscle training has a reasonable evidence base for strengthening the breathing muscles and reducing how hard breathing FEELS. What it does not do is raise VO2 max, improve oxygen saturation, or help you acclimatise. It changes the sensation of breathing effort more than the underlying capacity.
respiratoryTrainer.altitudeRelevance: There is a genuine mechanistic case at altitude: acclimatisation works largely by breathing much more, so your respiratory muscles work far harder up high than at sea level. Stronger ones plausibly help. The direct evidence for altitude performance specifically is thin, so hold this as reasonable rather than proven.
respiratoryTrainer.bestSideEffect: The instruction sheet's step 5 — abdominal pressure, slow forceful exhale — is the same mechanic as pressure breathing, the altitude technique already in your plan. Practising it at home on a device makes it automatic on the switchbacks. That may be the most transferable thing about it.
respiratoryTrainer.timing: Effects need roughly 4-6 weeks. Starting Jul 27 puts you in useful territory by early September, which is comfortably before Oct 2. Good timing.
respiratoryTrainer.protocol: Typical research protocol is about 30 breaths twice a day, at a resistance where 30 breaths is hard but completable. Generic devices are not calibrated, so set it by feel rather than trusting the dial numbers.
cautions: Do NOT use it shortly before or during a hike. Pre-fatiguing your breathing muscles ahead of a big effort works against you.

Reflux: forceful inspiration against resistance lowers pressure inside the chest, which can encourage reflux. Given your history, use it well away from meals, sitting upright rather than lying down, and stop if it aggravates symptoms.
The sheet says consult a doctor if you have health conditions — worth a sentence at the Diamox appointment given the reflux.
Clean with warm water after use and do not share the mouthpiece.
respiratoryTrainer.expectations: Same honesty as the beet juice: do not expect to feel a difference. If it works, it shows up as breathing feeling less desperate on a steep grade at altitude, not as more power.

energyBudget.concept: Your glycogen tank holds roughly 1,800 usable calories and does not get bigger with training in any way that matters here. Your burn rate is 300-356 cal/hr, steady across ten hikes. So every hike is a simple race: does the clock outlast the tank plus whatever you put in?
energyBudget.glycogenNote: Muscle glycogen roughly 1,400-2,000 cal plus liver roughly 400. Individual and approximate, but the shape of the conclusion does not depend on the exact figure.
energyBudget.keyInsight: Blue Sky is a five hour hike and your tank alone lasts five and a half. That is the entire reason it feels good — the trail is shorter than your fuel, so how much you eat barely matters. Every hike where you hit the wall was longer than the tank.

sanJacinto.verdict: Ran dry at hour 9.8 of an 11.1 hour hike. The 'vegetable' descent was not a mystery, a fitness limit or altitude — it was an empty tank, arriving roughly 80 minutes before the car.

saturday.note: Devils Slide at twelve hours will cost roughly 4,269 calories. Your tank covers 1,800 of it. That leaves about 2,470 you have to carry and actually swallow — which is 206 calories an hour just to reach the car, and 275 to arrive with something left. This is the number that decides Saturday.

gelMath.plan: Increasing from 4 gels to 6 on Devils Slide.
gelMath.verdict: Good move, but do not mistake it for the solution. Six gels is 600 calories. Devils Slide at twelve hours needs about 2,470 beyond your tank as a floor and 3,300 to arrive with reserves. Six gels cover 18-24% of that. The other 2,700 has to come from real food, and that is the part worth planning.
cautions: Check the caffeine on your flavour. Six gels is roughly 210 mg if they are 35 mg each, but 420 mg if they are 70 — and caffeine is a reflux trigger for you.
Always take a gel WITH water, never dry. A concentrated gel pulls fluid into the gut, which is what makes bloating worse.
Do not stack two gels close together. Alternate gel and solid food, which is how the schedule below is built.
Six gels is 150 g of maltodextrin and fructose. Your gut handled four with mild bloating; six is a real step up, so Saturday is the test rather than Whitney.

saturdayFuelPlan.hike: San Jacinto via Devils Slide (or Marion Mountain)
saturdayFuelPlan.principle: Anchored to the clock, not to landmarks. Landmarks fail the moment you are slower than planned; the 45-minute buzzer does not. Use the map to check you are on pace, not to decide when to eat — that is exactly how the fuelling ended up back-loaded last time.
saturdayFuelPlan.landmarkCheck: Your San Jacinto chart gives a better checkpoint than any trail map: you summited at hour 6.4 of 11.1. For a twelve-hour Devils Slide, aim to be on the summit around hour 6.5 to 7. If you are past hour 8 at the top, you are looking at a long descent on a dwindling tank — eat more, not less, and consider turning around if the arithmetic stops working.
saturdayFuelPlan.sodiumNote: This plan carries 2,594 mg of sodium in food. Salt tabs and electrolyte mix supply the rest — aim 700-1,000 mg per litre of fluid on top of this.
saturdayFuelPlan.headroom: Lands at 289 cal/hr — comfortably above the 206 floor and just past the 275 target, which is the right side to err on. Carry it all; if you finish the day with one bar and an orange left over, that is a well-judged pack, not waste.

sanJacintoProfile.source: Exact, from the FIT file (8,835 records downsampled to 41 points). No longer traced by eye.
sanJacintoProfile.insight: The chart pins down what the numbers could only imply. You summited at hour 6.4 and had 4.7 hours of descending left. Your tank ran dry at hour 9.8 — which is 3.4 hours into that descent, with roughly 1.3 hours still to walk. That is the 'vegetable' stretch, and it is now located precisely on the graph.
sanJacintoProfile.paceObservation: The blue pace trace is also worth looking at: it is a dense forest of spikes from end to end, swinging between near-stopped and brisk over and over. That is the surge-and-stop pattern rendered as data, and it is most extreme on the descent — exactly where you had the least fuel to absorb it.
sanJacintoProfile.transferToDevilsSlide: Devils Slide is a similar single-peak shape with comparable gain over more distance, so expect the same profile stretched: summit somewhere around hour 6.5 to 7 of a twelve-hour day, and five hours of descending after it. Your old fuelling put two gels across a 6.4 hour climb — one every three and a bit hours. That is the gap the new plan closes.
sanJacintoProfile.traceCheck: My hand-traced summit estimate was 6.4 h. The FIT says 6.40. The tracing was sound, which is mildly reassuring about the earlier analysis.

caffeinePlan.confirmed: Your gels are the 35 mg version, so six gels is 210 mg at most — not the 420 mg I flagged as a possibility.
caffeinePlan.strategy: Caffeine-free for the first two gels, caffeinated for the last four. That puts every milligram in the second half, which is where your own evidence says it pays: the Roctane that transformed your last 2-3 miles arrived at the end, not the start.
why: Caffeine peaks 30-60 minutes after you take it and has a half-life around five hours. Front-loading means it is largely gone by the descent — the exact stretch where you ran empty.
Perceived effort is highest late. Caffeine works on perceived effort more than on power, so late is when it earns its place.

Four caffeinated gels from hour seven gives 140 mg total, and because caffeine clears slowly the amount actually on board peaks at about 112 mg around hour eleven — right in the worst stretch of the descent. Modest dose, precise timing.
caffeinePlan.whitneyRule: Day 1 you arrive at Trail Camp in the afternoon and have to SLEEP at 12,000 ft, where your sleep is already compromised — your San Jacinto score was 39 after a hard day at sea level. So: caffeine-free gels only after about midday on Oct 1, and save the caffeinated ones for the summit push on Oct 2. A 35 mg gel at 4pm still leaves roughly 17 mg on board at 9pm, and on summit eve that is a trade worth avoiding.
caffeinePlan.packingTip: Mark the two kinds differently — a dot of marker on the caffeine-free ones. At hour nine you will not want to be squinting at small print.

rimToRim.name: Grand Canyon Rim to Rim
rimToRim.whyItChangesThings: This was never in the training log and it should have been. You walked 24.45 miles with 6,289 ft of climbing and 5,246 ft of descending in a single sixteen-hour day, starting at 3:12 AM, and finished it. That is MORE distance and MORE ascent than Whitney's two days combined.
rimToRim.vsWhitney: Whitney is roughly 22 miles, 6,200 ft up and 6,200 ft down, spread over two days. Rim to Rim was 24.45 miles and 6,289 ft up in one. The distance and the vertical are not the question — you have already done more.
whatWhitneyAddsThatThisDidnt: Altitude. Rim to Rim topped out at 8,262 ft. Whitney's summit is 14,505 — over 6,000 ft higher, and that is the one variable this hike did not test at all.
Sleeping high. Rim to Rim was a single push with no night at elevation. Whitney has you sleeping at 12,000 ft before the hardest part.
Pack weight. A day pack there against roughly 30 lb of overnight kit on Whitney Day 1.
rimToRim.reassurance: The honest read: your endurance base is not the limiting factor and never was. Sixteen hours on your feet is a demonstrated capability. What remains untested is narrow and specific — altitude, a night at 12,000 ft, and pack weight. That is a much better position than the log suggested, and it is worth knowing before Saturday.

stoppedTimeAnalysis.headline: The breakpoint is real, and it sits exactly where your fuel runs out.
stoppedTimeAnalysis.interpretation: Across 99 activities the pattern is monotonic and unmistakable. Under three hours you stop 5% of the time. Between three and five, 13%. Five to six, 24%. Six to nine, 33%. Beyond nine hours, 50%. The correlation between duration and stopped time on hikes over three hours is r = +0.77, which is strong.
stoppedTimeAnalysis.theCoincidenceThatIsNot: Your glycogen tank lasts about 5.5 hours at your burn rate. The stopped-time curve bends sharply between five and six hours. Those two numbers landing in the same place across 31 independent long hikes is the best evidence in this entire project — and it is evidence for YOUR explanation, not any of mine. Under the tank duration you barely stop. Past it, stopping escalates fast.
stoppedTimeAnalysis.whatItPredicts: If the model is right, Saturday's fuel plan should hold your stopped time near the 3–5 hour band's 13% rather than the 55% you ran on San Jacinto — even though the hike is twelve hours. That is a clean, falsifiable prediction. If stopped time still comes in above 40% on full fuelling, the model is wrong and we look elsewhere.

bigDaySleep.finding: Sleep collapses on the night of every long effort. Across the six longest days the night-of average is 3.8 hours against 6.8 the night before and 6.3 typical. Rim to Rim produced 2.3 hours at a score of 18; San Jacinto 3.1 hours at 40; Jun 6 gave 3.3 hours at 26.
bigDaySleep.whitneyImplication: This is the sharpest argument yet for arriving at Trail Camp with reserves. Day 1 ends at 12,000 ft and summit day depends on the sleep that follows it — and the pattern says a hard day costs roughly half a night even at sea level. Altitude, cold and a UL1 tent will not improve on that. Front-loaded fuelling, an early finish and no caffeine after midday all buy sleep that night, which is the real currency for Oct 2.

recovery.trend: Over the last nine weeks HRV has risen from about 49 to 53 while resting heart rate has eased from 65 to 64, dipping to 61 in early July. Both point the same way: the training is being absorbed rather than accumulating as strain.

spo2Gap.problem: Pulse oximetry has produced 3 readings in 304 days of health data — effectively off. For an altitude objective this is the most useful sensor on the watch and it is not running.
spo2Gap.action: Enable it in the Fenix under Health & Wellness, Pulse Ox, set to All Day or at least During Sleep. Doing it now builds a sea-level baseline over the next nine weeks, so the readings at Cottonwood and Trail Camp mean something instead of being the first ever taken. Baseline from the three existing readings is 94-96%.

wheyProtein.verdict: Not during the hike. Yes within an hour after it, and yes on weekdays.

why: Carbohydrate is the limiting fuel on a climb, not protein. Where studies show a benefit from adding protein during endurance exercise, it is mostly in trials where carbohydrate intake was already too low — the correct fix there is more carbohydrate, not a protein substitute. The evidence for a performance gain when carbs are adequate is weak.

Gut capacity on a long day is finite and it is already the bottleneck. Protein and fat slow gastric emptying, and there is a standing record of bloating with four gels and gut distress after long efforts, plus reflux.
Every calorie of shake displaces a calorie of carbohydrate at the exact hours the tank is emptying. On the current pattern that trade goes the wrong way.

afterHike.recommendation: Yes — this is the good use
afterHike.detail: 25-40 g of whey with carbohydrate inside about 60 minutes of finishing. Liquid is easier than food when appetite is gone after a big day, which it reliably is. Whey plus a banana, or whey stirred into the usual rice and curd, both work.

weekdays.detail: Daily protein target is 117-146 g and Jul 30 stood at 34 g by mid-morning. One or two shakes closes most of that gap without cooking, and it does not compete with anything.

wheyProtein.caution: Whey is a common trigger for bloating in people who already get it. Test it on a weekday before relying on it after a big Saturday.

prediction.verdict: Improved by 8 points on a bigger day. Did not reach 40%. Directionally right, target missed — and the fuelling number below says why.

intake.note: Bread and bar computed from the labels he photographed. 174 cal/hr against a 250-300 target and 25 g carb/hr against 60-90. Absolute intake rose, but the day was bigger, so the RATIO barely moved: 54% of burn against ~50% on San Jacinto.

fluidSodium.note: Best sodium day on record by a wide margin — 7 SaltStick plus a Liquid IV. Still 539 mg/L against a 700-1,000 target. 6 L carried is 13.2 lb of water alone, which is most of why the pack felt heavy.

whatHappened: Woke early, incomplete bowel movement in two attempts, poor sleep before a 3:45 am start.
Fuelled steadily on the way up. Ran out of gels near the top and the mood changed as soon as they were gone.
GI event at 9,700 ft on descent requiring a stop.
Questioned at 9,000 ft whether to do Whitney at all and whether to stop training.
Then covered the last three miles in 22, 21 and 23 minutes — about 2.7 mph.

readsOnIt.point: The legs were never the problem
readsOnIt.detail: Average HR 140 on 16.12 mi and 4,511 ft, against 146 on San Jacinto's 13.24 mi and 4,590 ft. Lower heart rate on a bigger day is a fitness gain, not a loss. Body Battery drained only 6 points across 11.6 hours.

readsOnIt.point: The last three miles are the proof
readsOnIt.detail: 22, 21, 23 minutes per mile — about 2.7 mph — at the end of an 11.6 hour day, after the low point. His own read is correct: the energy was there and the mind did not believe it. Something external broke the spell and the body immediately delivered.

readsOnIt.point: Wanting to quit at hour eight is a blood-glucose event, not a verdict
readsOnIt.detail: Intake ran 1,723 kcal behind burn. Low carbohydrate availability degrades mood and decision-making directly and reliably — that is the mechanism, not a character flaw. The thought arrived when the gels ran out and left when the oranges and a distraction went in. Treat it as a symptom on the same footing as the cramping calves.

The 40 g bar looks like fuel and gives 9 g of net carbohydrate for 200 calories, two thirds of it fat. Ordinary sandwich bread gives 18 g net per slice — twice the whole bar, for half the calories. The Inked bread at 1 g net is a third case again. Three breads and bars in this project now, all counted as carbs, delivering 1, 9 and 18 g.

readsOnIt.point: The stomach has three named suspects
readsOnIt.detail: Five gels over the day is a heavy concentrated-carbohydrate load; the 40 g bar carries 6 g of fibre and a gastrointestinal-discomfort warning on the flap, which usually means sugar alcohols; and four oranges at 9,000 ft added fructose, fibre and acid at the worst moment. The incomplete morning bowel movement is a fourth. Only one of those needs removing to find out which.

whatToChange: Carry more gels than felt necessary. Running out was the pivot of the whole day.
Drop the 40 g bar from the trail list. It is fat and fibre wearing a fuel label.
Real food carbs on the way up: sandwich bread at 18 g net a slice, dates, banana. Cheaper on the gut than a fifth gel.
Sodium worked — keep the SaltStick and Liquid IV protocol, and push toward 700 mg/L.
Carry 4.5 L rather than 6 and plan a filter stop. 13.2 lb of water is 45% of the Whitney Day 1 pack target, spent on something a GRAYL can refill.
thingsDoneRight: Beet juice at 4 am for a 6:15-6:30 start — 2.25 to 2.5 h before moving, which is the plasma-nitrite peak window. The timing protocol was followed correctly.
30 g protein shake (Okyo) immediately after finishing — exactly the post-hike use that was recommended, in the window that matters.
7 SaltStick tablets plus a Liquid IV: 2,965 mg total, the best sodium day on record.

fuelPlanV2.builtFrom: Devils Slide Aug 2, where intake ran 174 cal/hr and 25 g carb/hr.

target.why: Not 60-90 g/hr. That is race guidance and jumping from 25 straight to 60 invites exactly the GI event that already happened at 9,700 ft. The gut adapts to what it is asked to absorb, so 45-55 on Aug 15, 60 by September.

biggestSingleFix.detail: 5.5 L of plain water was drunk on Aug 2. At 60 g per 750 ml bottle, four bottles is 240 g of carbohydrate with no extra chewing, no gut bulk and nothing to run out of in a pocket. That one change is larger than every gel carried. Plain water stays in the reservoir — mix goes in bottles, or the bladder grows things.

switchToLMNT.verdict: Yes. LMNT is the right call.
switchToLMNT.why: LMNT is 1,000 mg sodium per stick against roughly 500 for Liquid IV, plus 200 mg potassium and 60 mg magnesium. Aug 2 landed at 539 mg per litre against a 700-1,000 target, and that was already the best sodium day on record. Doubling the sodium per stick closes it without adding volume.
switchToLMNT.carbCaveat: LMNT carries no carbohydrate. It is a sodium tool, not a fuel tool — it does not replace the carb drink, it goes alongside it.
switchToLMNT.dose: Target 700-1,000 mg per litre drunk, not a fixed stick count. At 5 L that is 3,500-5,000 mg total. Three LMNT sticks is 3,000 mg; food and a few SaltStick cover the rest. Do not simply stack 4 LMNT on top of 7 SaltStick — count the total.
switchToLMNT.diamoxNote: Acetazolamide is a diuretic. On any day he takes it, fluid and sodium both go up, and the per-litre target becomes a floor rather than a goal.

precisionFuel.verdict: Yes, switch. It is a genuine upgrade for two specific reasons, not marketing.

gel.vsGU: GU Roctane is 21-23 g. Same number of sachets in the pocket, 36% more carbohydrate. Eight PF gels is 240 g where eight GU is ~176 g.

drinkMix.whyItMatters: This one product hits both open targets at once. He needed 700-1,000 mg sodium per litre and got 539 on Aug 2, and he needed carbohydrate in the water he was already drinking. At label strength, 3 L of mix is 180 g of carbohydrate and 3,000 mg of sodium with no gels and no tablets.
drinkMix.math: 750 ml bottle at label strength = 45 g carb + 750 mg sodium. Mix to 1 L for 60 g.

precisionFuel.keepLMNT: Still worth having. The PF mix covers sodium inside the fluid; LMNT is the top-up when sweat rate outruns drinking, and it is the simpler thing to hand to a partner. Do not run PF mix AND 3 LMNT AND 7 SaltStick — count the total against 700-1,000 mg per litre drunk.

waterFilter.problem: GRAYL UltraPress needs real force on the press. He says it is hard now and will be worse at Trail Camp, which is correct — at 12,000 ft, cold, tired, filling for two people and for cooking.
waterFilter.answer: Gravity, not squeeze. A gravity system is the only category that needs no force at all: hang the dirty bag and walk away. Squeeze filters just move the effort from your palms to your hands.

flowRates.Platypus QuickDraw: ~1.5 L/min in the field, not the advertised 3

recommendation.pick: Gravity — CNOC Vecto 3 L + the Sawyer Squeeze already in the plan sheet, or a Platypus GravityWorks 4 L
recommendation.why: Zero force. Hang it while setting up the tent. The Sawyer is already owned per the gear sheet, so the CNOC bag is the only purchase and it is the cheap route.
Easy squeeze and fast. BeFree has the best real-world flow but clogs soonest.
Grams, no moving parts, no force. Chemical treatment is the answer when a filter clogs or freezes.

twoWarnings: SILT: Trail Camp water is silty and silt clogs squeeze and gravity filters alike. Pre-filter through a bandana into the dirty bag and backflush often.

FREEZING DESTROYS FILTERS and a frozen one is unsafe rather than merely slow. October at 12,000 ft will freeze one left out. The filter sleeps in the bag with him — this is already in the freeze mitigations for the bladder and now covers the filter too.
waterFilter.keepGrayl: The GRAYL is a purifier, not just a filter — it handles viruses, which the others do not. Worth keeping for travel. It is simply the wrong tool for filling 6 L at altitude with tired arms.
